newsitem.title: USA: Advanced units lower mortality for babies - study.
newsitem.headline: Advanced units lower mortality for babies - study.

text.p: High-risk newborns stand a better chance of survival at no increase in health costs if their mothers deliver in a hospital with a busy, advanced neonatal intensive care unit, researchers said on Tuesday.

Babies born in a hospital with a Level III neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) -- which provides a full range of specialised newborn care -- did significantly better than babies transferred promptly to such a facility after birth or those treated in a lower-level NICU, the researchers found.

A research team led by Ciaran Phibbs, a health care economist with the Veterans Affairs Palo Alto Health Care System in California, found that costs of care for children born at hospitals with large Level III NICUs were not more than those for infants born at hospitals with lower-level NICUs, which do not provide the full range of services.

"Concentration of high-risk deliveries in urban areas in a small number of hospitals that could provide Level III NICU care has the potential to decrease neonatal mortality without increasing costs," the researchers wrote in an article published in The Journal of the American Medical Association.
The study was also presented on Tuesday at the American Medical Association's science reporters conference here.

The researchers tracked 53,229 infants born in non-federal hospitals in California in 1990 who were classified as likely NICU admissions. The study showed that infants born in a hospital with a Level III NICU that treated at least 15 patients a day had a 38 percent less chance of dying than newborns born at other hospitals.

"Hospitals with Level III NICUs have a full range of obstetric and neonatal services available at all times. These hospitals also have staffs who are experienced at working with complex cases, which seems to increase the infant's odds of survival," said Phibbs, who is also a consulting assistant professor of health research at Stanford University.
The study disclosed that only 35 percent of extremely premature and high-risk infants -- those born after less than 28 weeks gestation -- were born at Level III institutions.
The study also found that infants insured by Health Maintenance Organisations (HMOs), by public insurance and those with no insurance have significantly higher mortality.

While poverty may partly explain the higher mortality for those with public or no insurance, this did not apply to those insured by HMOs, the study said. "The cause of these higher mortality rates warrants further investigation," it said.
